claims.text: A Bayesian-optimization framework trained on a minimal, strategically selected experimental dataset can accurately and efficiently predict multiple fusion and liquid-phase properties across HEA composition space.
The targeted properties are melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacity.
Near-equiatomic HEAs typically have single- or dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructures before melting.
A sparse set of DSC and drop-calorimetry measurements can provide the experimental basis for the proposed model.
Bayesian optimization can iteratively identify the most informative HEA compositions for subsequent fusion-property measurements.
High-temperature DSC, dilatometry, or drop calorimetry is feasible across HEA melting ranges.
Short-range chemical reconfigurations occur in the liquid phase and can be captured through thermodynamic descriptors.
Descriptors of liquid short-range chemical reconfiguration can guide surrogate-model predictions for novel HEA compositions.
Each targeted new measurement updates the Bayesian model and improves its predictive power.
Improved prediction arises by linking composition and structure to thermodynamic behavior.
Melting temperature can be predicted to within approximately 15 K.
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacity can be predicted to within 5–10% of measured values for compositions covered by the training data.
CALPHAD-based high-throughput methods have previously been used for HEA design and composition-space screening.
Previous CALPHAD-based high-throughput methods lack adaptive sampling.
The method is applicable when compositions and phases remain within its calibration range and accurate thermodynamic data are available.
Predictions are less certain at unexplored or highly complex compositional extremes.
Volume-change measurements near melting may have higher experimental variability.
Data sparsity in unusual compositions can reduce model fidelity.

DSC peak integration can determine fusion enthalpy and support derivation of fusion entropy, while dilatometry or X-ray scattering can determine melting-associated volume change and drop calorimetry can determine liquid heat capacity.
Systematic prediction errors greater than 15% for multiple out-of-sample HEAs would invalidate the proposed approach.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability and quantitative performance are restricted to the calibration range or training-covered compositions, but the proposed invalidation test deliberately uses compositions beyond that range. Failure there would not decisively refute the approach within its stated boundary.

Melting-temperature performance is specified as an absolute error of approximately 15 K, whereas the falsification rule applies a generic relative error threshold of 15% to all properties; these criteria are not equivalent.
